title: SCIM 2.0
heading: SCIM 2.0 — provisioning into the directory
notAnEndpoint: This page is not a SCIM endpoint; a real server publishes none of it.
verified: These endpoints require a credential, and it is verified. They create and DELETE accounts. An access token carries a SCIM scope only when {token} issued it to a client whose oauthAllowedScope declares it, and only while the client still does; a Basic password is verified against the person's directory entry; Digest is not offered; and only the signed-in owner of an existing account may register a HOBA key for it.
verifiedNotRequired: These endpoints require a credential — except that it is currently turned off here, so right now they do not, and it is verified. They create and DELETE accounts. An access token carries a SCIM scope only when {token} issued it to a client whose oauthAllowedScope declares it, and only while the client still does; a Basic password is verified against the person's directory entry; Digest is not offered; and only the signed-in owner of an existing account may register a HOBA key for it.
development: These endpoints require a credential, and almost nothing is checked about it. They create and DELETE accounts, which is why this is the one surface in this service that asks at all. This realm is in development mode, and the schemes below are permissive, bar one: an access token carries a SCIM scope only when {token} issued it to a client whose oauthAllowedScope declares it, and only while the client still does. Beside that, any username with any password but invalid passes Basic, any username passes Digest with one shared password, and anybody can register a HOBA key for any name. A turnstile, not a lock — what it buys is that a client's 401, 403 and challenge-response paths can be run at all.

active: And active: false disables the account — it writes the password-policy lock pwdAccountLockedTime, every door then refuses the person, and everything they held is ended, exactly as the Disable button on their /admin/users page does.

authOpen: RFC 7644 section 2 defines no credential of its own — it delegates to TLS and to RFC 7235 and NAMES six schemes. All six are here. Its one SHALL is that a provider indicate its schemes in WWW-Authenticate, which every 401 from these endpoints does; its one MUST is that a provider be able to map an authenticated client to an access control policy, which is the list under the table. The realm is {realm}. Discovery (/ServiceProviderConfig, /ResourceTypes, /Schemas) is OPEN — a client has to be able to read which schemes exist before it can use one.
authClosed: RFC 7644 section 2 defines no credential of its own — it delegates to TLS and to RFC 7235 and NAMES six schemes. All six are here. Its one SHALL is that a provider indicate its schemes in WWW-Authenticate, which every 401 from these endpoints does; its one MUST is that a provider be able to map an authenticated client to an access control policy, which is the list under the table. The realm is {realm}. Discovery (/ServiceProviderConfig, /ResourceTypes, /Schemas) is closed too (scim.authDiscovery).
scopesText: The two OAuth scopes are {read} and {write}, published in scopes_supported in both discovery documents. Digest offers {algorithms}. HOBA keys are registered at {hoba}.
